keyVerseText: Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham; for a father of many nations have I made thee. Abraham: that is, Father of a great multitude
rootMeaning: The name אַבְרָהָם (ʼAbrâhâm) is etymologically contracted from אָב (ʼâb), meaning 'father,' combined with an unused root likely signifying 'to be populous.' This gives the name the literal sense of 'father of a multitude' or 'chief of a multitude.' The root אָב conveys not only a biological father but also a chief or founder of a family or clan, emphasizing leadership and origin. Thus, the name carries a depth beyond a simple personal name, highlighting Abraham's role as a progenitor and leader of many.
usageInScripture: The word אַבְרָהָם appears 175 times in Scripture, with translations ranging from 'And Abraham' (38 times) to 'of Abraham' (26 times) and 'unto Abraham' (19 times), showing its frequent use as a proper noun referring to the patriarch himself. The consistency in translation as a personal name, often in relational or possessive forms, underscores Abraham's central role in biblical narrative and covenantal history. The variety of prepositional phrases attached to his name reflects his active participation in God's promises and dealings with His people.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding the original meaning of אַבְרָהָם as 'father of a multitude' enriches our grasp of God's covenantal promise that Abraham would be the progenitor of many nations, not merely a single family line. This name change from Abram to Abraham marks a divine appointment to a global mission, highlighting God's sovereign plan to bless all nations through Abraham's descendants. Theologically, Abraham exemplifies faith and obedience, becoming a model for believers who are grafted into this spiritual lineage through Christ. His name encapsulates God's faithfulness in fulfilling promises that transcend ethnic and temporal boundaries.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 17:5 declares, 'Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham; for a father of many nations have I made thee.' This verse explicitly connects the name change to God's promise of multiplication and blessing. The word אַבְרָהָם here is not merely a label but a divine identity that defines Abraham's role as the patriarch of a vast multitude, reinforcing the covenantal scope and God's purposeful plan for his descendants.
